agenda: Reports of the Secretary-General on the Sudan and South Sudan
members: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

steps.intent: Our primary objectives are to extend the targeted sanctions and the South Sudan arms embargo for an additional 12 months, as well as the mandate of the Panel of Experts, to curb the destabilizing flow of weapons amid the escalating conflict and transitional delays in South Sudan. We anticipate significant pushback from the A3+1 (Algeria, Sierra Leone, Somalia, Guyana) as well as Russia and China, who consistently advocate for lifting or easing the arms embargo to accommodate the Necessary Unified Forces and South Sudan's sovereignty. The challenge will be maintaining the necessary nine affirmative votes while preventing vetoes, requiring firm adherence to the established review benchmarks while resisting efforts to prematurely terminate the sanctions regime.

messages.Algeria: Algeria reiterates the long-standing position of the African members that the arms embargo on South Sudan is counterproductive in its current form, as it severely hinders the transitional Government's capacity to operationalize and equip the Necessary Unified Forces. Sanctions must serve as flexible, temporary tools that support peace implementation rather than constrain legitimate state security capacity. Unless the draft incorporates meaningful adjustments—specifically facilitating the equipping of the Necessary Unified Forces—Algeria will not be able to vote in favour.
messages.China: China has consistently maintained that Security Council sanctions on South Sudan have outlived their original rationale and severely impede the government's ability to equip the Necessary Unified Forces and maintain national security. The Council should demonstrate patience and encouragement toward the youngest UN Member State, especially given the severe economic shocks and spillover of the conflict in Sudan, rather than exerting unilateral and excessive pressure. Unless this draft creates concrete pathways toward lifting the arms embargo and reflects the realities and constraints on the ground, China will not be able to support it.
messages.Denmark: Denmark strongly supports the renewal of the arms embargo, targeted sanctions, and the mandate of the Panel of Experts as indispensable tools for protecting civilians and advancing peace in South Sudan. We commend the United States for circulating a robust text that rightly maintains pressure on the parties to meet the established benchmarks. Our proposed adjustments seek to ensure appropriate emphasis on accountability, the protection of civic space, and women's full, equal, and meaningful participation as South Sudan prepares for its extended transitional timeline.
messages.France: France thanks the United States for circulating this balanced draft renewing the South Sudan sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts, which remain essential instruments to protect civilians, reduce armed violence, and foster conditions for sustainable peace. We firmly support the renewal of the arms embargo and targeted measures, and would welcome a clearer reference to the urgent need to advance transitional justice and accountability under Chapter V of the Revitalized Agreement. We stand ready to work constructively with the penholder and all Council colleagues towards the swift adoption of this text.
messages.Greece: Greece strongly supports the renewal of the arms embargo, targeted sanctions, and the mandate of the Panel of Experts as critical tools to curb violence and protect civilians in South Sudan. We appreciate the penholder's balanced text, including the retention of clear, objective benchmarks for reviewing the measures. Our minor proposal aims to reinforce the imperative of full respect for international humanitarian law and the protection of humanitarian space amidst an alarming humanitarian crisis.
messages.Guyana: Guyana, working closely with the A3+, emphasizes that sanctions must serve as an adaptable tool to support peace rather than an impediment to the implementation of the Revitalized Agreement. The Council should heed the consistent appeals of the African Union and IGAD by providing practical relief for the equipping and deployment of the Necessary Unified Forces and establishing a tangible pathway towards lifting the arms embargo. We also urge the penholder to reflect the profound economic and humanitarian shocks South Sudan faces due to the crisis in Sudan, including the critical disruption of the oil pipeline.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan believes that targeted measures and arms embargoes must not serve as blunt or punitive tools, nor should they hinder the legitimate capacity of the South Sudanese authorities to maintain law and order and deploy the Necessary Unified Forces. It is essential that the Council provide a clear, realistic pathway toward easing and ultimately lifting these measures based on objective benchmarks, while giving due weight to the severe economic shocks caused by the conflict in Sudan. We also urge the penholder to maintain a constructive and balanced tone regarding engagement with the host government, which is indispensable for ensuring full cooperation on the ground.
messages.Panama: Panama fully supports the draft resolution renewing the targeted sanctions, the arms embargo, and the mandate of the Panel of Experts, which are vital tools for curbing violence, illicit arms flows, and gross human rights violations in South Sudan. We particularly welcome the robust language addressing conflict-related sexual violence, the protection of civilians, and unimpeded humanitarian access. To ensure consistency with the Council's established sanctions architecture, we propose a minor reference to resolution 2664 (2022) on humanitarian exemptions, and look forward to voting in favor of the text.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea appreciates the United States' leadership in preparing this draft resolution renewing the South Sudan sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts. Given the volatile security environment, heightened humanitarian distress compounded by the Sudan conflict spillover, and delays in implementing the Revitalized Agreement, maintaining the arms embargo and targeted measures remains essential to protecting civilians. We strongly support the benchmark-guided framework and look forward to working closely with the penholder toward a swift adoption.
messages.Russian Federation: The arms embargo and sanctions regime against South Sudan have long become outdated and counterproductive, severely constraining Juba's sovereign capacity to equip the Necessary Unified Forces and respond to acute security threats, including spillover from the conflict in Sudan. The draft must focus on establishing a realistic, time-bound roadmap toward completely lifting the arms embargo rather than multiplying punitive demands and finger-pointing against the transitional authorities. If our legitimate concerns and the sovereign interests of South Sudan are not reflected, the Russian Federation will not be in a position to support this resolution.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone, aligned with the A3+ and the African Union position, underscores that the arms embargo in its current form hinders South Sudan's ability to effectively equip and deploy the Necessary Unified Forces, which are vital for national stability and preparing for elections. The Security Council must recognize the severe exogenous shocks South Sudan is enduring from the conflict in Sudan, including the oil pipeline shutdown and massive influx of returnees. We urge the penholder to introduce targeted exemptions for the Necessary Unified Forces and outline a realistic pathway toward lifting the sanctions regime.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia strongly supports the draft resolution and the renewal of the arms embargo, which remains indispensable for civilian protection and mitigating the risk of escalating violence. We thank the United States for the balanced text and propose modest additions to underline accountability, transitional justice, and the protection of humanitarian workers. Slovenia stands ready to vote in favour of the text.
messages.Somalia: Somalia underscores the principled position of the African Union and IGAD that the arms embargo poses significant impediments to the full operationalization and equipping of the Necessary Unified Forces, which are vital for South Sudan's security transition and long-term stability. While we recognize the importance of targeted measures, sanctions regimes must not hinder state capacity-building or the primary responsibility of sovereign authorities to protect civilians. We urge the penholder to accommodate regional calls by providing clear exemptions for the unified forces and outlining a genuine, expedited pathway toward lifting the embargo.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom strongly supports the draft resolution circulated by the United States to renew the arms embargo, targeted sanctions, and the mandate of the Panel of Experts for a full 12 months. Given the fragile security landscape, the continued prevalence of conflict-related sexual violence, and persistent delays by the transitional authorities in meeting key benchmarks, maintaining this regime is vital for the protection of civilians and regional stability. We will work closely with the penholder to ensure the integrity of the arms embargo and the Panel's mandate is preserved against any efforts to dilute the text during consultations.

steps.summary: As penholder, the United States has introduced targeted adjustments to secure the necessary broad Council majority while maintaining the core integrity of the sanctions regime and the Panel of Experts. The revised draft directly accommodates the A3+ and regional concerns by granting an explicit exemption for non-lethal military equipment, technical assistance, and training for the Necessary Unified Forces, recognizing the economic shocks from the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline shutdown, and toning down operative paragraph 9, while incorporating accountability, transitional justice, and civic space priorities from European and like-minded partners.

messages.Algeria: Algeria appreciates the penholder's inclusion of an exemption for non-lethal equipment, but this falls short of what is urgently needed to enable the graduation and operationalization of the Necessary Unified Forces. Restricting the NUF to non-lethal equipment impedes the transitional government from fulfilling its primary security responsibilities under the Revitalized Agreement. We urge the penholder to align the text with the clear positions of the African Union and IGAD by allowing notified transfers for the NUF and establishing a clear trajectory towards lifting the arms embargo.
messages.China: China appreciates the penholder's inclusion of the exemption for non-lethal equipment and training for the Necessary Unified Forces in OP1. However, sanctions must serve as a means rather than an end, and prolonged sanctions and arms embargoes severely hinder South Sudan's state capacity-building and security sector reform. The draft still maintains an overly rigid benchmark framework and fails to properly heed the consistent calls of the African Union, IGAD, and the host government for the lifting of the arms embargo; unless these concerns are fully addressed, China will abstain in the vote.
messages.Denmark: Denmark expresses its sincere appreciation to the penholder for accommodating our proposals on accountability, the protection of civic space, and women's full, equal, and meaningful participation. The draft text strikes a necessary and principled balance by renewing vital sanctions measures, preserving the reporting integrity and safety of the Panel of Experts, and maintaining a clear benchmarked framework for review. Denmark fully supports the text in its current form and is prepared to vote in favour.
messages.France: France thanks the United States for accommodating our proposal regarding transitional justice and the Hybrid Court in preambular paragraph 4. The current draft strikes an appropriate balance by maintaining the necessary pressure of the arms embargo and targeted sanctions while outlining clear benchmarks for their review. France fully supports the text as currently drafted and stands ready to vote in favour.
messages.Greece: Greece thanks the United States for accommodating our proposal on international humanitarian law and unhindered humanitarian access in preambular paragraph 6. The current draft strikes an appropriate balance by renewing targeted sanctions and the arms embargo while maintaining a clear, benchmarked path for review and exempting support for the Necessary Unified Forces. Greece fully supports the text as drafted and looks forward to voting in favour.
messages.Guyana: Guyana expresses its sincere appreciation to the penholder for constructively accommodating our key priorities in Revision 1, in particular the carve-out for non-lethal equipment and training for the Necessary Unified Forces, the recognition of AU and IGAD perspectives, and the acknowledgement of the severe economic consequences of the oil pipeline shutdown. These additions strike an essential balance between maintaining necessary oversight and supporting South Sudan's state capacity and security transition. In this spirit of constructive engagement, Guyana is pleased to support the draft resolution as currently formulated.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan appreciates the penholder's incorporation of our concerns regarding the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline and the operationalization of the Necessary Unified Forces (NUF). To ensure internal consistency across Security Council sanctions regimes, we reiterate that the mandate of the Panel of Experts should be aligned with the duration of the sanctions measures themselves, expiring on 31 May 2026 rather than prejudging future renewals. Furthermore, in line with the repeated appeals of the African Union and IGAD, the Council should provide a practical pathway for the transitional government to properly equip the NUF so that it can fulfill its primary security and peacebuilding responsibilities.
messages.Panama: Panama thanks the United States for accommodating our proposal regarding resolution 2664 (2022) and for maintaining a balanced text that supports peace, accountability, and the protection of civilians in South Sudan. The current draft reflects our shared priorities, including unhindered humanitarian access and benchmarks for review, and Panama is prepared to vote in favour of the resolution as drafted.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea thanks the United States for accommodating our proposal in preambular paragraph 6 regarding accountability for attacks against humanitarian and United Nations personnel. We fully support the current draft resolution, which strikes a balanced approach by renewing critical sanctions measures and the mandate of the Panel of Experts while maintaining clear benchmarks and exemptions to support the Necessary Unified Forces. We look forward to voting in favor of this text.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation maintains its principled stance that the arms embargo has long outlived its usefulness and directly hinders the South Sudanese authorities from equipping the Necessary Unified Forces and ensuring security, particularly amid serious regional spillover from Sudan. We cannot accept the penholder's persistent practice of using sanctions texts to lecture Juba, including the biased and hostile framing in OP9 targeting the host authorities. Unless the draft genuinely accounts for the unified position of the African Union and IGAD calling for the lifting of the embargo, our delegation cannot support this resolution.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone commends the penholder for constructively accommodating our primary concern by including the crucial exemption for non-lethal equipment and training for the Necessary Unified Forces in paragraph 1, as well as acknowledging the severe economic impact of the oil pipeline disruption. In line with the position of the A3+ and regional organizations, we believe paragraph 3 should more clearly indicate a pathway toward progressively easing or lifting these measures as benchmarks are met. Incorporating these final improvements will ensure the text genuinely assists South Sudan's transition and security architecture.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia thanks the United States for incorporating our proposals on transitional justice under Chapter V and the applicability of international humanitarian law regarding attacks on humanitarian and UN personnel. The revised draft strikes an appropriate balance by renewing vital arms embargo measures to protect civilians while maintaining transparent benchmarks for review and necessary safeguards. Slovenia fully supports the text as currently drafted and stands ready to vote in favour.
messages.Somalia: Somalia welcomes the penholder's constructive efforts in Rev 1, particularly acknowledging the role of the AU and IGAD as well as introducing an exemption for the Necessary Unified Forces. However, to genuinely support South Sudan's transition and security architecture, the text should accurately reflect IGAD and AU calls and provide a workable mechanism for equipping the unified forces. We remain committed to engaging constructively to ensure the resolution supports state-building and the full implementation of the Revitalized Agreement.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom strongly supports the draft resolution renewing the South Sudan sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts. The text maintains the essential architecture of the arms embargo and targeted sanctions, which remain critical for the protection of civilians, mitigating conflict-related sexual violence, and deterring further escalation. We appreciate the United States' continued leadership on this file and stand ready to vote in favour of the text as drafted.

steps.summary: The United States revised the draft resolution to accommodate regional sensitivities by referencing African Union and IGAD calls regarding the arms embargo in PP8 and signaling a clear trajectory for easing measures tied to benchmarks in OP3. Crucially, the text maintains essential non-lethal parameters for NUF exemptions and preserves the reporting integrity, safety, and unhindered access of the Panel of Experts. The resolution commands a solid affirmative majority of at least 10 votes without provoking a permanent member veto.

reasons.Algeria: Algeria maintains its consistent position alongside the African Union and IGAD that the arms embargo on South Sudan is counterproductive and impedes the transitional government from equipping the Necessary Unified Forces, and because the penholder rejected key amendments to exempt materiel for the NUF, Algeria abstains as it did on resolution 2731 (2024).
reasons.China: China consistently maintains that Security Council sanctions, particularly the arms embargo, constrain South Sudan's legitimate security capacity-building and ignore the calls of the African Union and IGAD for their lifting or easing. Since the penholder rejected China's proposed amendments to establish a clearer pathway for lifting the sanctions and to remove unbalanced pressure on the transitional government, China abstains.
reasons.Denmark: Denmark supports the renewal of the South Sudan sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts as essential tools to curb illicit arms flows, protect civilians, and incentivize progress on the peace agreement benchmarks. In line with Council practice, Denmark votes in favour without delivering an explanation of vote prior to the voting procedure.
reasons.France: France consistently supports the renewal of the South Sudan sanctions regime and Panel of Experts mandate to curb violence, protect civilians, and maintain pressure for the implementation of the peace agreement, especially with its requested transitional justice language retained.
reasons.Greece: Greece consistently supports the renewal of the South Sudan sanctions regime and the arms embargo to prevent further violence, protect civilians, and uphold international humanitarian law, aligning fully with its EU partners and previous voting record.
reasons.Guyana: Guyana supported the draft resolution following the accommodation of key priorities regarding support for the Necessary Unified Forces and the economic impact of the oil pipeline shutdown, and will therefore vote in favour. In line with standard practice, any explanation of vote will be delivered after the adoption.
reasons.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the renewal of the targeted sanctions regime and arms embargo with calibrated exemptions for the Necessary Unified Forces to foster peace and stability in South Sudan. While Pakistan regrets that its proposals to align the Panel of Experts' mandate with the sanctions regime and further ease equipment restrictions were not incorporated, these concerns do not preclude a positive vote and will be addressed in an explanation of vote after adoption.
reasons.Panama: Panama consistently supports the renewal of targeted sanctions and the arms embargo to prevent the proliferation of weapons and protect civilians in South Sudan, while upholding the humanitarian exemptions established under resolution 2664.
reasons.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea consistently supports the South Sudan sanctions regime and the work of the Panel of Experts as vital tools to stem the illicit flow of weapons and protect civilians, while welcoming the inclusion of strong accountability language for attacks against humanitarian and UN personnel.
reasons.Russian Federation: Russia maintains its consistent stance of abstaining on the South Sudan sanctions renewal, as the arms embargo hinders the legitimate capacity of the South Sudanese authorities to deploy the Necessary Unified Forces and ignores repeated calls from Juba, the African Union, and IGAD for its lifting. Furthermore, our proposed modifications regarding the Panel of Experts and regional calls were not adequately accommodated by the penholder.
reasons.Sierra Leone: The penholder accommodated Sierra Leone's and the A3's priority textual proposals regarding the AU and IGAD positions on the arms embargo, exemptions for the Necessary Unified Forces, and language on the progressive easing of sanctions. Having had its key negotiating concerns addressed, Sierra Leone votes in favour of the resolution and reserves its explanation of vote for after the adoption.
reasons.Slovenia: Slovenia supports the renewal of the South Sudan sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts as essential tools to stem the flow of weapons, protect civilians, and advance the implementation of the Revitalized Peace Agreement. In line with its consistent voting record on this agenda item and its position in negotiations, Slovenia votes in favour of the draft resolution.
reasons.Somalia: Somalia supports the renewal of the sanctions regime with the incorporated exemptions for the Necessary Unified Forces and the explicit recognition of AU and IGAD calls regarding the arms embargo, in line with its constructive engagement throughout negotiations.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom strongly supports the renewal of the South Sudan sanctions regime and arms embargo to prevent the further proliferation of weapons, protect civilians, and incentivize progress on peace agreement benchmarks. In line with Council practice, the UK will deliver its explanation of vote after the adoption.
reasons.United States of America: As the penholder and author of the draft resolution, the United States voted in favour of renewing the South Sudan sanctions regime and the Panel of Experts mandate, delivering a statement introducing and defending the necessity of the measures prior to the vote.

before.United States of America:
Thank you, Madam President. 

As the penholder, the United States has put forward this draft resolution to extend the South Sudan sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts. The measures renewed today—including the targeted arms embargo, travel ban, and asset freeze—remain vital tools for stemming the flow of weapons into a volatile environment and promoting peace, stability, and accountability.

South Sudan continues to face severe political, security, and humanitarian challenges, compounded by persistent delays in implementing the Revitalized Peace Agreement, escalating violence, pervasive conflict-related sexual violence, and attacks on humanitarian personnel. In this fragile context, flooding South Sudan with weapons would only deepen the suffering of its people and further endanger regional stability.

This resolution is carefully balanced and calibrated. It includes clear exemptions to support the training and deployment of the Necessary Unified Forces and reaffirms our commitment to reviewing, easing, or lifting these measures as tangible progress is made against the established benchmarks. The text also takes into account the immense economic and humanitarian pressures created by the spillover of the conflict in Sudan.

The sanctions regime is not intended to be permanent, nor is it punitive; it is designed to protect civilians and foster an environment where lasting peace and democratic governance can take root. We urge all Council members to support this draft resolution.

after.Algeria:
Madam President,

Algeria wishes to explain its vote on the resolution just adopted.

Our abstention today reflects our consistent and principled position regarding the South Sudan sanctions regime, particularly the arms embargo. 

Sanctions are not an end in themselves; they are temporary tools intended to support peace processes and encourage positive political transitions. When they cease to serve that intended purpose and instead hinder the legitimate efforts of a sovereign State to build its institutions and provide security for its people, they must be reassessed and adjusted.

The transitional Government of South Sudan continues to face tremendous challenges, further compounded by the devastating spillover effects of the ongoing conflict in the Sudan, including an influx of hundreds of thousands of refugees and returnees, and the severe economic crisis triggered by the disruption of critical oil infrastructure. In such a fragile environment, the primary imperative must be supporting State capacity, consolidating stability, and completing the implementation of the transitional security arrangements under the Revitalized Agreement.

In that regard, the arms embargo continues to impede the ability of the transitional Government to fully train, equip, and deploy the Necessary Unified Forces, which are essential to extending State authority, protecting civilians, and stabilizing the country ahead of the planned democratic transition. While illicit arms continue to proliferate through informal channels, the legitimate armed forces face restrictions that undermine their capacity to address intercommunal violence and ensure national security.

Regional organizations, including the African Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), have repeatedly called for the lifting or substantial easing of these measures to facilitate the implementation of the peace agreement. We deeply regret that this Council has once again missed an opportunity to adequately heed these regional calls and meaningfully adapt the sanctions regime to the reality on the ground.

Madam President,

Algeria remains steadfast in its solidarity with the people of South Sudan. We reaffirm our commitment to South Sudan’s sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity, and we urge all South Sudanese stakeholders to expedite the implementation of the Revitalized Agreement. However, to help South Sudan achieve lasting peace and stability, the international community and this Council must prioritize constructive engagement, capacity-building, and partnership rather than prolonged punitive measures.

I thank you.
after.China:
Madam President,

China abstained in the voting on the draft resolution just adopted. I would like to take this opportunity to explain China’s position.

China has consistently maintained that Security Council sanctions are merely a means, not an end, and should serve the political settlement of relevant issues. Sanctions should never be used as a blunt instrument to exert pressure, nor should they be maintained indefinitely. Instead, they should be adjusted or lifted in a timely manner in light of the evolving situation on the ground.

At present, South Sudan is at a critical juncture in advancing its political transition and national peace process. The Revitalized Transitional Government of National Unity is making unremitting efforts to implement the Revitalized Agreement and the Roadmap, advance security sector reform, and build State capacity. South Sudan faces daunting challenges, including the economic fallout and spillover effects of the ongoing conflict in neighbouring Sudan, severe humanitarian constraints, and logistical hurdles. Under these circumstances, what South Sudan needs most from the international community is constructive encouragement, financial and technical support, and capacity-building assistance, rather than undue pressure and sanctions.

For a long time, the African Union, IGAD, and African countries have repeatedly called on the Security Council to lift or ease the arms embargo on South Sudan. The continued imposition of an arms embargo severely restricts the South Sudanese Government’s ability to train, equip, and deploy the Necessary Unified Forces, impairs its sovereign capacity to protect civilians and maintain security, and creates obstacles to the peace process. Regrettably, the text just adopted fails to give adequate consideration to the legitimate security needs and sovereignty of South Sudan, nor does it fully reflect the reasonable calls of African regional organizations. 

China has always supported the African people in resolving African issues in African ways. We call on the Security Council to heed the voices of South Sudan and regional countries, carefully review the impact of sanctions, and establish clear, realistic, and achievable benchmarks with a view to lifting the sanctions and the arms embargo as soon as possible. China will continue to work with the international community and regional partners to play a constructive role in supporting South Sudan’s peace, stability, and sustainable development.

Thank you, Madam President.
after.Denmark:
Thank you, Madam President.

Denmark voted in favour of the resolution just adopted, renewing the targeted sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts on South Sudan. 

Our vote reflects our firm conviction that the arms embargo remains an indispensable tool to curb the flow of weapons into an already volatile environment, protect civilians, and prevent further escalation of violence. With more than nine million people in South Sudan in dire need of humanitarian assistance and the devastating spillover effects from the conflict in Sudan, injecting more arms into the country would only worsen the suffering of the population.

We remain deeply concerned by persistent delays in implementing the key benchmarks of the Revitalized Peace Agreement, the shrinking of civic and political space, and the continued postponement of elections. We urge the Transitional Government to demonstrate genuine political will, disburse the necessary resources, and create the conditions for inclusive, free, and fair elections, ensuring the full, equal, and meaningful participation of women and youth.

Accountability is paramount. The alarming reports of widespread human rights violations and abuses, particularly conflict-related sexual violence, recruitment of children, and deliberate attacks against humanitarian workers, are unacceptable. Those responsible must be held accountable, and we urge swift progress towards the establishment of the Hybrid Court and other transitional justice mechanisms.

At the same time, we welcome that this resolution provides calibrated exemptions to support the training and deployment of the Necessary Unified Forces, acknowledging the Transitional Government's capacity-building needs for security sector reform. 

Sanctions are not an end in themselves; they are a means to promote peace, stability, and accountability. Denmark remains fully committed to supporting the people of South Sudan on their path toward lasting peace.

I thank you.
after.Greece:
Madam President,

Greece voted in favour of the resolution just adopted, extending the South Sudan sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts for an additional year. We thank the United States, as penholder, for its constructive engagement throughout the negotiation process.

Our affirmative vote reflects our steadfast conviction that the targeted measures renewed today—most notably the arms embargo—remain essential tools for curbing the flow of illicit weapons into an already volatile environment, preventing further escalation of violence, and protecting innocent civilians. These measures are not an end in themselves, nor are they intended to impede the legitimate state-building efforts of the South Sudanese authorities. In this regard, we welcome the calibrated language in the resolution, including the exemptions that allow for the supply of non-lethal equipment and technical assistance to support the deployment and training of the Necessary Unified Forces.

Madam President,

Greece remains deeply concerned by the sluggish pace of implementation of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement and the postponement of elections to December 2026. While the challenges facing South Sudan are formidable—compounded by the severe spillover effects of the devastating conflict in Sudan and the recent shutdown of the oil pipeline—lasting peace cannot be achieved without genuine and sustained political will. The Transitional Government must take urgent, concrete steps to allocate the necessary resources for electoral preparations, advance security sector reform, and operationalize transitional justice mechanisms, including the Hybrid Court.

We also reiterate our grave concern over ongoing violations of international humanitarian law and widespread human rights abuses, in particular conflict-related sexual violence and attacks against civilians. The continuing targeting of and bureaucratic impediments imposed on humanitarian workers and United Nations personnel are unacceptable and must cease immediately. Ensuring full, safe, and unhindered humanitarian access is an obligation, not an option.

In conclusion, Greece reaffirms its full support for the people of South Sudan and will continue to back all international and regional efforts—particularly by the African Union and IGAD—aimed at achieving sustainable peace, stability, and democratic governance in South Sudan.

Thank you.
after.Pakistan:
Madam President,

Pakistan voted in favour of the resolution just adopted, extending the South Sudan sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts for another year.

Our vote reflects our continued commitment to supporting peace, stability, and security in South Sudan, as well as our belief that curbing the illicit flow and destabilizing accumulation of weapons is essential to reducing violence, protecting civilians, and fostering an environment conducive to political dialogue. South Sudan continues to face acute political, security, and humanitarian challenges, which have been severely compounded by the spillover effects of the devastating conflict in neighbouring Sudan, including the influx of returnees and refugees and the disruption of critical economic lifelines such as the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline. 

At the same time, Pakistan maintains a principled position on Security Council sanctions. Sanctions are not an end in themselves, nor should they be indefinite. They must be periodically reviewed, objectively assessed against realistic benchmarks, and adjusted to the realities on the ground to ensure they do not hinder legitimate state-building, national security sector reform, or socio-economic development. 

In this regard, we welcome the provisions in the resolution that exempt non-lethal military equipment, technical assistance, and training intended for the support of the Necessary Unified Forces. The deployment and operationalization of these forces are critical to enabling the Government of South Sudan to assume its primary responsibility for the protection of civilians and maintaining security throughout the country. 

We also take note of the repeated calls made by the African Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) regarding the easing and eventual lifting of the arms embargo. The Council must remain receptive to the voices of the region and the concerns of the host country. 

As South Sudan moves towards the conclusion of its transitional period and preparations for elections in December 2026, the international community must step up its engagement, provide vital humanitarian and developmental assistance, and support the full and timely implementation of the Revitalized Peace Agreement.

I thank you.
after.Russian Federation:
Madam President,

The Russian Federation abstained in the vote on the draft resolution submitted by the United States to extend the sanctions regime against South Sudan and the mandate of the Panel of Experts.

Our position of principle on Security Council sanctions is well known. Sanctions must never be an end in themselves, nor should they be used as an instrument of political pressure or punishment against sovereign Governments. Council measures must reflect the actual developments on the ground, encourage positive political processes, and be subject to regular review and clear benchmarks leading to their timely modification and eventual lifting.

Unfortunately, the text just adopted once again fails to take into account the realities on the ground and the legitimate needs of the authorities of South Sudan. For years, the arms embargo has severely impeded Juba’s ability to build and equip its national security structures, particularly the Necessary Unified Forces, which are vital to ensuring security, protecting civilians, and stabilizing the country. Without adequate resources, arms, and equipment, the national authorities cannot fully implement the security arrangements stipulated in the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement.

We must also remind colleagues of the persistent calls by the African Union, IGAD, and the countries of the region to lift or substantially ease the sanctions and arms embargo on South Sudan. Disregarding the voice of regional organizations directly undermines the principle of "African solutions to African problems."

Moreover, South Sudan today faces tremendous socio-economic and humanitarian strain, heavily exacerbated by the conflict in neighbouring Sudan, the influx of hundreds of thousands of refugees and returnees, and the severe economic shock resulting from the disruption of the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline. At this critical juncture, South Sudan requires genuine solidarity, capacity-building, and economic assistance from the international community, not punitive measures that hinder state-building.

As for the Panel of Experts, we reiterate that its work must strictly adhere to the standards of impartiality, objectivity, and verifiability of information, rather than serving narrow geopolitical agendas.

Russia remains committed to supporting the people and Government of South Sudan in their pursuit of lasting peace, security, and sustainable development.

I thank you.
after.Sierra Leone:
Madam President,

Sierra Leone voted in favour of the resolution just adopted, which renews the South Sudan sanctions regime, including the targeted arms embargo, and extends the mandate of the Panel of Experts. We thank the penholder, the United States, for its engagement and constructive consultations throughout the negotiation process.

Sierra Leone’s vote in favour is guided by our principled commitment to the protection of civilians, the prevention of further atrocities, and the maintenance of regional peace and security. South Sudan continues to face acute challenges, marked by localized violence, widespread conflict-related sexual violence, and persistent attacks against civilians and humanitarian workers. As a country that has experienced the devastating consequences of armed conflict, Sierra Leone understands all too well the urgent need to halt the flow of weapons that fuel internal strife and exacerbate human suffering, particularly among women and children.

At the same time, Sierra Leone has consistently maintained that sanctions are not punitive ends in themselves, but rather tools intended to support peace processes and foster an environment conducive to political dialogue and national stability. In this regard, we welcome the adjustments and flexibility reflected in the resolution, notably the exemption for the supply of non-lethal military equipment, technical assistance, and training intended solely for the Necessary Unified Forces. Equipping and training these forces is critical to advancing security sector reform, consolidating national security architecture, and successfully implementing the 2018 Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in the Republic of South Sudan.

We also take note of the profound external shocks confronting South Sudan, particularly the severe spillover effects of the ongoing war in Sudan. The influx of hundreds of thousands of refugees and returnees, coupled with the critical disruption of the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline, has placed immense economic and fiscal burdens on the transitional authorities and severely strained public services. 

In this context, Sierra Leone aligns itself with the broader calls of the African Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development for the international community to accompany South Sudan constructively. We reiterate the necessity for the Security Council to keep these measures under regular review, with clear and realistic benchmarks, so that sanctions can be calibrated and progressively adjusted as progress is achieved on the ground.

Finally, we urge the Revitalized Transitional Government of National Unity and all political stakeholders in South Sudan to demonstrate genuine political will, fulfill their commitments under the Revitalized Agreement and the Roadmap, allocate necessary resources to key electoral and constitutional bodies, and advance transitional justice mechanisms under Chapter V. Only through inclusive dialogue, accountability, and the full participation of women and youth can South Sudan achieve durable peace, stability, and democratic governance.

I thank you, Madam President.
after.Slovenia:
Madam President,

Slovenia voted in favour of the resolution renewing the South Sudan sanctions regime, including the targeted arms embargo and the mandate of the Panel of Experts. We thank the United States, as penholder, for its efforts throughout the negotiations.

Our vote reflects Slovenia’s unwavering commitment to the protection of civilians and the prevention of further violence in South Sudan. In a context marked by persistent subnational violence, widespread human rights violations—including alarming levels of conflict-related sexual violence and the recruitment of children—and catastrophic humanitarian needs, the arms embargo remains an indispensable tool. Its objective is clear: to stem the flow of weapons into an already volatile environment and prevent further suffering.

At the same time, sanctions are not punitive; they are calibrated to encourage compliance with international obligations and support the peace process. We welcome the provisions in this resolution that accommodate the logistical and training needs of the Necessary Unified Forces, recognizing the importance of completing security sector reform.

Madam President,

The extension of the transitional period to December 2026 must not lead to complacency. We urge the Revitalized Transitional Government of National Unity to demonstrate genuine political will by allocating the necessary resources to key electoral and constitutional bodies, establishing the required security environment, and expanding civic and political space, ensuring the full, equal, and meaningful participation of women. 

We also remain profoundly alarmed by the safety of humanitarian personnel and persistent obstructions to aid delivery. Attacking humanitarian workers and looting relief supplies are unacceptable and may constitute war crimes. All parties must uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law and ensure unhindered humanitarian access to the millions facing acute food insecurity, a crisis now severely exacerbated by the devastating conflict in neighbouring Sudan.

Finally, Slovenia reaffirms its support for the Panel of Experts, whose independent reporting is vital to our work. We stand with the people of South Sudan in their pursuit of lasting peace, justice, and accountability.

I thank you.
after.Somalia:
Madam President,

Somalia voted in favour of the resolution just adopted, renewing the sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts on South Sudan. 

Our vote reflects Somalia’s steadfast commitment to peace, security, and stability in South Sudan and the wider Horn of Africa. As a sister nation and fellow member of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), Somalia remains deeply invested in supporting the people and the Transitional Government of South Sudan on their path toward lasting peace, national reconciliation, and democratic consolidation.

We welcome the adoption of this resolution, particularly the provisions that facilitate support, non-lethal equipment, and training for the Necessary Unified Forces. The graduation and full deployment of unified security forces are critical components of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement and are essential for establishing state authority, protecting civilians, and maintaining law and order.

At the same time, drawing from our own national experience, Somalia firmly believes that sanctions measures must not be punitive or indefinite. They should serve as targeted tools to support peace and must be calibrated to reflect progress on the ground. We underscore the need for the Security Council to maintain regular reviews and clear, realistic benchmarks that pave the way toward the eventual lifting of the arms embargo, in line with the calls of the African Union and IGAD, so as not to hinder South Sudan’s legitimate state-building and security sector reform efforts.

We also express our profound concern over the deteriorating humanitarian situation in South Sudan, which has been severely exacerbated by the devastating conflict in Sudan, the influx of refugees and returnees, and the disruption of critical economic lifelines such as the Greater Nile Oil Pipeline. We urge the international community and humanitarian partners to scale up assistance to address this immense humanitarian burden.

In conclusion, Somalia reaffirms its full support for the Revitalized Agreement as the viable foundation for sustainable peace. We encourage the Transitional Government and all South Sudanese stakeholders to demonstrate the necessary political will to implement the remaining transitional tasks and prepare for credible, peaceful, and inclusive elections. Somalia will continue to stand in solidarity with South Sudan, working through IGAD, the African Union, and this Council to help achieve the peaceful and prosperous future that the South Sudanese people rightfully deserve.

I thank you.
after.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort:
Thank you, Madam President.

The United Kingdom voted in favour of this resolution, renewing the South Sudan sanctions regime and the mandate of the Panel of Experts for another year. We thank the United States for its diligent leadership as penholder during these negotiations.

At a time when South Sudan continues to face acute political fragility, pervasive subnational violence, and severe humanitarian distress—compounded by the devastating conflict in neighbouring Sudan—the Council's renewal of these measures is essential.

The targeted arms embargo remains a vital tool to reduce the influx of weapons, protect civilians, and deter violence against vulnerable populations. In a country where millions face severe food insecurity and where attacks on humanitarian workers and peacekeepers continue unabated, unconstrained flows of weapons would only deepen the crisis.

The United Kingdom remains deeply concerned by the lack of progress in implementing the key benchmarks of the Revitalized Peace Agreement and the Roadmap. We urge the Transitional Government to demonstrate genuine political will and allocate the necessary resources to advance security sector reform, operationalize transitional justice mechanisms—including the Hybrid Court—and establish the conditions necessary for peaceful, free, and credible elections. South Sudanese authorities must also guarantee civic and political space, protect the rights of women and girls, and urgently address impunity for gross human rights violations and widespread conflict-related sexual violence.

Furthermore, we call on the South Sudanese authorities to immediately halt bureaucratic impediments, taxes, and fees on humanitarian operations, and to ensure full, safe, and unhindered access for all humanitarian personnel who risk their lives daily to deliver life-saving aid.

Finally, we reaffirm our full support for the work of the Panel of Experts, whose independent reporting is indispensable for the Council's oversight. The United Kingdom will continue to stand with the people of South Sudan in their pursuit of lasting peace, stability, and accountability.

I thank you.
